questions.question: On a military system, every subject and file carries a sensitivity label; a cleared user cannot relax protection on her own files because the rules are fixed by central policy. Which access-control model is this?
questions.explanation: Mandatory access control imposes system-wide label-based rules that users cannot override — the opposite of owner-controlled permissions — suiting high-security environments.

questions.question: On a Unix desktop, the owner of report.txt runs chmod 640 to decide herself who may read it; no administrator or central policy is involved. Which access-control model is in play?
questions.explanation: Under discretionary access control, owners grant or revoke rights on their own objects — flexible, but a compromised or careless owner can leak data.

questions.question: A hospital grants permissions to roles like 'doctor' and 'nurse' rather than assigning them to each of its 3,000 employees; a hire simply inherits a role's rights. Which access-control model is this?
questions.explanation: RBAC maps users to roles and roles to permissions, collapsing thousands of individual grants into a few role definitions — far easier to administer and audit.

questions.question: DEP/NX stops an attacker from running injected shellcode, so the exploit instead chains short 'ret'-ending sequences already present in libc to build its computation. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: ROP reuses existing code gadgets whose addresses end in ret, stitching them via the stack — defeating data-execution prevention because no new code is injected.

questions.question: A compiler emits a random value between a function's locals and its saved return address, checking it before every return and aborting if it changed. Which defense mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: A stack canary sits where a buffer overflow must overwrite it before reaching the return address; a mismatch proves corruption and the process aborts before returning.

questions.question: A browser runs each tab's renderer with a stripped-down syscall set and no direct filesystem access, so a compromised renderer cannot reach the rest of the machine. Which containment technique is this?
questions.explanation: Sandboxing executes untrusted code inside a restricted environment — limited syscalls, no direct file or device access — so a breakout only buys an empty cell.

questions.question: An OS refuses to load a kernel driver whose signature fails verification against the vendor's certificate, catching a tampered binary before it runs. Which integrity technique is this?
questions.explanation: Code signing binds a binary to its publisher via a digital signature; any post-signing modification breaks the signature, letting the OS reject tampered or unsigned code.

questions.question: In SELinux, a root-owned httpd_t process is still denied write access to a shadow_t file because policy binds allowed operations to the pairing of subject type and object type. Which mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: Type enforcement labels subjects and objects with types and permits access only where an allow rule matches — confining even root daemons to their domain.

questions.question: A consultant reads BankA's confidential file, and the system then automatically denies her access to rival BankB's data, since the banks compete and her access history now forbids it. Which model enforces this?
questions.explanation: The Brewer-Nash (Chinese Wall) model dynamically blocks reads across conflict-of-interest classes once a subject has accessed a competitor's data.

questions.question: The seL4 kernel was not merely tested: its implementation was mathematically proven to satisfy a formal specification of its security properties. Which assurance method does this represent?
questions.explanation: Formal verification uses mathematical proof to show a system meets its specification for all inputs — stronger than any test suite, and the basis of seL4's security claims.

questions.question: A SECRET-cleared subject copies classified notes into an UNCLASSIFIED log file, leaking them to anyone. Which Bell-LaPadula property did this downward write violate?
questions.explanation: The *-property forbids writing to a lower level, stopping secrets from flowing downward; combined with the simple security property (no read up), it preserves confidentiality.

questions.question: A Trojan process is barred from writing to any lower-clearance file, so it instead modulates how long it holds a shared lock, letting an unclassified accomplice measure the delays and reconstruct bits. Which channel type is this?
questions.explanation: Covert timing channels signal information through observable delays on shared resources, bypassing every access-control check since no policy-labeled object is ever written.

questions.question: A phone keeps biometric keys where even a fully rooted OS cannot read them, inside a hardware-isolated world with its own minimal OS alongside the normal one. What is this environment?
questions.explanation: A TEE — e.g., ARM TrustZone or Intel SGX — runs code and data in hardware-separated memory the rich OS cannot touch, so secrets survive a compromised kernel.

questions.question: In world-writable /tmp, user Mallory tries to delete Alice's scratch file and gets EPERM even though Mallory has write permission on the directory itself. Which mode bit caused this?
questions.explanation: With the sticky bit set on a directory, only a file's owner (or root) may delete or rename entries inside — which is why /tmp is mode 1777.

questions.question: A payroll system requires one officer to create a payment and a different officer to approve it, so no single insider can commit fraud alone. Which security principle does this implement?
questions.explanation: Separation of duties splits a sensitive operation across multiple parties, forcing collusion for abuse — a core fraud deterrent in financial and administrative systems.

questions.question: A subject cleared at SECRET tries to read a TOP SECRET file. Which Bell-LaPadula property denies this?
questions.explanation: The simple security property forbids reading above one's clearance; the star property separately forbids writing down.

questions.question: A process classified LOW-integrity attempts to modify a HIGH-integrity object. Which Biba-model rule blocks it?
questions.explanation: Biba's *-integrity axiom forbids writing to a higher integrity level, protecting trusted data from contamination.

questions.question: An auditor must quickly answer 'who can access file X?' Which access-control representation, ACL or capability list, answers this directly?
questions.explanation: ACLs are stored per object and enumerate every subject's rights on it; capability lists are stored per subject.

questions.question: An attacker swaps a symbolic link between a privileged program's permission check and its file open. Which vulnerability class is this?
questions.explanation: TOCTOU races exploit the gap between checking a condition and acting on it, changing the target in between.

questions.question: An exploit hardcodes a libc gadget address that works once, then crashes on every rerun because each execution loads libraries at a different base. Which mitigation is enabled?
questions.explanation: ASLR randomizes the base addresses of the stack, heap, and shared libraries on every run, so any hardcoded exploit address becomes useless after one attempt.
